title: Iron focusing and sulphur-driven mineral formation regulate phosphorus sequestration in Lake Stechlin (NE Germany)
abstract: Abstract Iron (Fe) plays a key role in lake ecosystems by regulating the availability of phosphorus (P) as a limiting factor for primary production. This study investigates how microbial sulphate reduction in Lake Stechlin, a dimictic and initially oligotrophic lake in northeast Germany (zₘₐₓ = 69.5 m), has altered the mobility of Fe and P over several decades. Using long-term monitoring data combined with sedimentological investigations, the study examines long-term geochemical focusing, defined as the net accumulation of redox-mobilised Fe in the deepest basin driven by reductive dissolution, lateral transport, and re-precipitation. Under oligotrophic conditions prior to the 1960s, focusing of Fe toward the deepest site likely involved: (1) reductive dissolution of sedimentary Fe oxides in shallow areas, (2) diffusion of dissolved Fe into overlying water, (3) re-oxidation/complexation and stepwise lateral transport within the water column, and (4) final deposition and burial at the deepest zone. Chemical and mineralogical evidence indicates that Fe burial was facilitated by authigenic formation of stable Fe(II) minerals, most likely ankerite (CaFe[CO 3 ] 2 ) and vivianite (Fe 3 [PO 4 ] 2 ·8H 2 O). Fe enrichment at the deepest site has strongly weakened, coinciding with intensified pyrite (FeS 2 ) formation in anoxic littoral and profundal sediments. This shift was likely driven by sufficient supply of organic matter and elevated sulphate inputs, which stimulated microbial sulphate reduction. Elevated S/Fe ratios indicate that sulphide efficiently competed with P for binding to Fe, potentially increasing susceptibility to external and internal P loading.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Preferential sedimentation of elements such as iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) has been documented in numerous lacustrine (Delfino et al.  7 ; Ostendorp and Frevert  38 ; Schaller and Wehrli  45 ; Naeher et al.  37 ; Scholtysik et al.  47 ,  48 ) and marine environments (Wijsman et al.  55 ; Raiswell and Anderson  41 ; Lenz et al.  32 ; Dijkstra et al.  8 ). This phenomenon was termed  geochemical focusing  by Schaller and Wehrli ( 45 ) in lacustrine systems and  shelf-to basin shuttle  by Lyons and Severmann ( 34 ) in marine systems. It involves the reductive dissolution of oxide-bound metals, particularly Fe or Mn, after initial deposition, followed by their diffusion into the overlying water column. Upon re-oxidation, these elements can be laterally transported by physical processes such as turbulent or eddy diffusion (Schaller and Wehrli  45 ; Raiswell and Anderson  41 ). Ultimately, they accumulate in topographic depressions of lakes or marine basins, where they may precipitate and become permanently buried as stable mineral phases.

One such mineral is vivianite (Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 ·8H 2 O), a stable Fe(II)-phosphate that is relatively resistant to early diagenetic transformation. Among the various organic and inorganic phosphorus (P) forms, vivianite is one of the most widespread authigenic P minerals in both lacustrine and marine sediments (Egger et al.  9 ; Rothe et al.  43 ) and can contribute substantially to long-term P sequestration in sediments (Jilbert and Slomp  21 ; Dijkstra et al.  8 ; Rothe et al.  43 ; Kubeneck et al.  25 ). Vivianite forms under reducing but non-sulphidic conditions and is commonly found associated with organic remains in Fe-rich sediments (Rothe et al.  43 ; Heinrich et al.  13 ).

Recent studies have demonstrated a close link between Fe enrichment and vivianite occurrence (e.g., Dijkstra et al.  8 ; Scholtysik et al.  48 ), highlighting the importance of vivianite formation for the sedimentary P sequestration (Jilbert and Slomp  21 ; Dijkstra et al.  8 ; Rothe et al.  43 ; Kubeneck et al.  25 ). Vivianite formation in lake sediments has only been observed at molar Fe:S ratios exceeding 0.5 (Rothe et al.  43 ), indicating that its formation is controlled by sulphate reduction and sedimentary Fe availability (Heinrich et al.  14 ). The immobilization of Fe through the formation of Fe sulphides (FeS x ) can be enhanced by several factors, including: (1) elevated organic matter inputs acting as an electron donor or as a source of sulphur (S); (2) atmospheric S deposition resulting from the combustion of S-rich lignite; or (3) inputs of S species from mine drainage or wetlands (reviewed by Zak et al.  59 ).

Despite its importance, the coupled geochemical cycling and sedimentary fate of Fe and P in lakes and marine basins remain incompletely understood. Previous studies have predominantly focused on highly eutrophic lakes (Schaller and Wehrli  45 ; Schaller et al.  46 ) or permanently stratified marine basins such as the Black Sea (Lenstra et al.  30 ) and the deep basins of the Baltic Sea (Scholz et al.  49 ; Lenstra et al.  31 ). In contrast, the role of Fe geochemical focusing in P retention and eutrophication dynamics in less eutrophic lake systems has received comparatively little attention.

To address this knowledge gap, we investigated sedimentary Fe, P, and S dynamics in Lake Stechlin (northeastern Germany), a deep, initially oligotrophic lake that has experienced pronounced eutrophication without a corresponding increase in external P loading (Gonsiorczyk et al.  11 ). Lake Stechlin has been the subject of numerous studies aiming to clarify the causes of its abrupt trophic shift (Selmeczy et al.  50 ; Gonsiorczyk et al.  11 ; Hilt et al.  16 ). As in many other deep lakes, climate change has led to prolonged stratification and enhanced oxygen depletion in the hypolimnion of Lake Stechlin (Kirillin et al.  22 ; Shatwell et al.  51 ). Without detailed consideration of the underlying processes, many studies about climate change impacts have postulated that increasing anoxia promotes internal nutrient loading by releasing additional redox-sensitive, Fe-bound P from sediments (Woolway et al.  57 ; Aeppli et al.  1 ). Accordingly, this study focuses on the role of sediments and potential changes in the Fe–P–S interaction in regulating the trophic status of lake ecosystems. By integrating sedimentological analyses along a water depth gradient with existing monitoring data on water quality, atmospheric S deposition, and sediment trap fluxes we tested the following hypotheses: (1) Excess P accumulation at the sediment surface under initially oligotrophic and non-sulphidic conditions promotes the formation of stable P phases (e.g., vivianite), upon burial and transition to anoxic conditions; (2) Increasing fixation of Fe as Fe-sulphide inhibits geochemical focusing and reduces sedimentary P sequestration capacity; and (3) The development of more sulphidic conditions is promoted by rising sulphate concentrations, as observed in Lake Stechlin and reported for other lakes worldwide.

The reconstruction of changes from sediment cores, combined with more recent observations, yields new insights into the role of Fe availability in regulating P sequestration under anoxic conditions, thereby influencing the trophic status of lake ecosystems.

sections.heading: Study site
paragraphs: Lake Stechlin is located in a sandy end-moraine region of northeastern Germany (53°09′N, 13°02′E; Fig.  1 ). It is a relatively large (4.23 km 2 ) and deep lake, with a mean depth of 23.3 m, a maximum depth of 69.5 m, and a total volume of 98.7 × 10 6  m 3  (Koschel and Adams  23 ). The entire shoreline and approximately 80% of the catchment area are covered by forest. The lake has no major natural surface tributaries; precipitation and groundwater dominate water balance (Holzbecher et al.  19 ). Lake Stechlin typically stratifies thermally from April through December and occasionally during winter. The water level has remained nearly constant since 1957 (Pöschke et al.  39 ). From 1966 to 1990, lake water was used for cooling a nuclear power plant, during which the theoretical water residence time was approximately 335 days (Koschel and Adams  23 ). Since 1990, the retention time has increased to over 40 years (Koschel and Adams  23 ). Lake Stechlin has been continuously monitored since 1960 (Wollrab et al.  56 ). The annual average total phosphorus (TP) concentration increased from 13 ± 3 µg P l −1  (1970–2010) to 37 ± 2 µg P l −1  (2016–2018) and reached 61 µg P l −1  in 2020 (Gonsiorczyk et al.  11 ). This rise in TP was accompanied by reduced transparency, elevated phytoplankton biomass, increased toxin-producing cyanobacterial taxa, and declining deep-water oxygen concentrations (Kröger et al.  24 ; Mehner et al.  35 ; Wollrab et al.  56 ). Bottom waters remained oxic until approximately 2011, when increasingly suboxic conditions (< 2 mg l −1 ) were observed toward the end of the summer stratification. Rising oxygen consumption rates in the hypolimnion subsequently caused an upward shift in the oxycline and a progressive expansion of the hypolimnetic oxygen-depleted zone. As a result of these changes, Lake Stechlin has transitioned from oligotrophic to mesotrophic conditions (Gonsiorczyk et al.  11 ). Fig. 1 Bathymetric map showing the sampling sites along a depth transect (yellow line) and the location of Lake Stechlin in Germany. The map was redrawn from Koschel and Adams ( 23 )

sections.heading: Sediments
paragraphs: Six sediment cores were retrieved from a short depth transect close to the deepest site (65  m, 64 m, 61 m, 56 m, 51 m, and 38 m) on 3 May 2018 (Fig.  1 ) to assess the geochemical focusing and its changes over recent decades. Sediment cores were collected using 60 cm long, 6 cm diameter PVC tubes with a Kajak gravity corer (UWITEC, Mondsee, Austria). Immediately after sampling, the cores were stabilized from above using foam, laid horizontally, and split lengthwise into two halves using stainless steel plates. One half was sub-sampled at 1 cm intervals, freeze-dried, and subjected to geochemical analyses (inductively coupled plasma–optical emission spectrometry—ICP-OES, X-ray diffraction—XRD, and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy—SEM–EDX), whereas the other half was used for XRF core scanning.

Three cores from the deepest site were examined in more detail, to reconstruct environmental changes over the past 100 years. Cores A1 and A2 were sampled on 24 August 2017 and core (B) sampled on 2 August 2018: Core A1 was used for element content analysis by ICP-OES, relative element composition using XRF, and mineralogical investigations via XRD and SEM–EDX. Core A2 was used for sediment dating based on heavy metals indicative for historical events during the last century, including mercury (Hg), zinc (Zn), lead (Pb), arsenic (As) and caesium ( 137 Cs). The radionuclides were stratigraphically correlated with core A1 using an offset correction based on cumulative dry mass per area. Core A2 was also scanned for its relative element composition using XRF. Core B was used for P and Fe fractionation to identify whether these elements form oxide or carbonate phases during early diagenesis.

sections.heading: Trap material
paragraphs: Data from a sediment trap monitoring program between 2010 and 2018 were used to assess recent Fe and P dynamics. The seasonal sedimentation patterns at two water depths were correlated with stratification and oxygen conditions, and comparison with the uppermost sediment layers were used to identify early diagenetic processes. Settling material was collected using two cylindrical sediment traps with a diameter of 9 cm, deployed at depths of 20 m and 60 m. The traps were poisoned with 0.13% formaldehyde to prevent microbial degradation (Lee et al.  29 ). Sampling intervals ranged from 1 to 2.5 months. Measurements were interrupted between 19 December 2012 and 24 March 2016, as well as during the following shorter periods: 24 September to 22 October 2009, 31 August to 13 October 2010, 13 June to 4 July 2016, and 19 December 2016 to 31 March 2017. Oxygen concentrations at 60 m water depth were measured using an O 2  probe (YSI 6600 V2-4, Xylem Analytics; Rye Brook, USA). The sedimentation rates of Fe and P were calculated by multiplying the element content by dry mass sedimentation rate (see Gonsiorczyk et al.  11  for details).

The trap-based Fe focusing is used here as an operational flux term describing the excess Fe flux at 60 m relative to 20 m during the monitoring period. Mechanical focusing was defined as the part of this excess Fe flux that can be explained by higher bulk particle sedimentation at 60 m, assuming the Fe content of material collected at 20 m. The remaining excess Fe flux was attributed to geochemical focusing, i.e. enrichment of settling material in Fe beyond that expected from bulk particle redistribution alone.

sections.heading: Porewater analysis
paragraphs: Sediment–water gradients were used to calculate sulphate reduction rates as input for the One-box model (see Sect. “ One-box Model ”) and to estimate the Fe mobility. Porewater profiles were obtained using dialysis samplers (peepers) made of acrylic glass, consisting of two parallel chambers at 58 discrete depths with a vertical resolution of 1 cm. The dual-row configuration is used for the analysis of different parameters at the same depth. The chambers are filled with deionized water, covered with a 0.2 µm pore size polysulfone membrane (HT-Tuffryn 200; Pall Gelman) and secured with a cover plate. Prior to deployment, the peepers were deoxygenated by storing them 24 h in an N 2 -filled container with continuous N 2  sparging. The devices were then lowered and inserted into the sediment using a rope. To ensure a stable vertical orientation at the sediment water interface (SWI), the peepers were mounted in a plastic frame (1 m 2 ) equipped with two stabilizing arms (details see Hupfer et al.  36 ).

Between 2008 and 2018, a total of ten profiles were collected from water depths of 69.5 m, 55 m, 30 m, and 17 m. Because concentration gradients in the overlying water are weak, only every second chamber was sampled. At approximately 8–10 cm above the sediment, the spatial resolution was increased to 1 cm. Sulphate samples were frozen until chemical analysis, while porewater Fe samples were acidified with 10 µl 2 M HCl. Sulphate reduction and flux rates were calculated using the Profile® software (Berg et al.  3 ). The area-weighted estimate was derived by assigning the mean rate from 58 m and 69.5 m to the 40–69.5 m depth zone (18% of lake area), and the mean rate from 17 and 30 m to areas shallower than 40 m (82% of lake area).

sections.heading: XRF core scanning
paragraphs: Sediment profiles for iron (Fe), titanium (Ti), calcium (Ca), sulphur (S), and silicon (Si) were determined using an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) core scanner (ITRAX, Cox Analytical Systems, Mölndal, Sweden; Croudace et al.  6 ). A chromium (Cr) tube was set to 30 kV and 30 mA, with an exposure time of 15 s per step and a resolution of 0.5 mm in the varved 0–7 cm section of the core from 69.5 m, and 1–2 mm in the other cores. Results were expressed as element-to-Ti ratios [cps cps⁻ 1 ] (cps: counts per second) to account for detrital input. The range of XRF signals obtained was 1600–40,000 cps for Fe; 130–1800 cps for Ti; 2000–80,000 cps for Ca; 16–254 cps for S; and 75–1200 cps for Si.

sections.heading: Determination of the elemental composition of solid phases and dissolved compounds
paragraphs: The contents of Ca, S, Fe, zinc (Zn), lead (Pb), and arsenic (As) in core A1 were determined following acid digestion with HNO 3 , HClO 4 , and HF using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES, iCAP 7400 Duo, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA). Precision and trueness were assessed using the international reference material SGR-1b (USGS), yielding values of 6% and −5%, respectively. Fe and Mn in the sediment traps, as well as P in core A1, were also measured using ICP-OES (iCAP 6300 Duo, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, USA) after acid digestion with 36% HCl and 65% HNO 3  in a 1:3 volumetric ratio, conducted in a high-pressure microwave system (MLS GmbH, Leutkirch, Germany). The corresponding precision and accuracy were 9% and 5%, respectively. The TP content of the dried trap material was determined spectrophotometrically following the digestion of 5–10 mg of dry sediment in a solution containing 2 ml of 5 mol/l H 2 SO 4 , 2 ml of 30% H 2 O 2 , and 20 ml of distilled water at 150 °C for 8 h. The total organic carbon (TOC) in sediments and trap material was estimated from loss on ignition (550 °C, 3 h) and dividing the resulting mass loss by two.

Relative XRF intensities were calibrated against the absolute elemental contents determined by ICP-OES for core A from a depth of 69.5 m. XRF signals were averaged for every 1 cm interval and plotted against the corresponding ICP-OES measurements. The resulting linear regression equations were used to calculate Ca, Fe, and S content for all cores. The regression coefficients were R 2  = 0.96 for Ca, R 2  = 0.97 for Fe, and R 2  = 0.95 for S. Prior to calibration, an offset correction was applied to the core halves used for XRF and ICP-OES analyses based on five prominent Ca and Mn peaks.

Concentration of porewater sulphate was determined using ion chromatography (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan), and dissolved Fe concentrations were measured by atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS; Perkin Elmer 3300, Rodgau–Juegesheim, Germany), with a relative standard error of less than 1%.

Mercury (Hg) content was determined using a DMA-80 Analyzer (MLS, Leutkirch, Germany). Calibration was performed against a certified reference material (CRM BCR-142R) and a standard reference material (SRM 2709 soil standard). Sample weights were approximately 100 mg. The precision and accuracy of the determinations were 6.6% and −13%, respectively. Analyses of artificial radionuclides ( 137 Cs and  241 Am) were conducted by gamma spectrometry using a Ge-well detector (GCW4021-7500SL-RDC-6-ULB) and processed with GENIE 2000 software (Canberra Industries Inc., USA). Counting statistics were better than 15% for  137 Cs and better than 20% for  241 Am activity. Radionuclide activities were calculated using decay-corrected standard reference materials: IAEA-447 ( 137 Cs) and IAEA-384 ( 241 Am). The following nuclides and energies were used for isotope quantification:  241 Am at 59.5 keV and  137 Cs at 661 keV.

sections.heading: Fractionation of phosphorus and iron
paragraphs: P and Fe species in selected sediment layers and sediment trap material were determined using a sequential extraction procedure originally developed by Psenner et al. ( 40 ) and modified by Hupfer et al. ( 20 ). The fractionation sequence included the following treatments: (1) 1 mol/l ammonium chloride (NH 4 Cl-P), representing porewater and loosely adsorbed P; (2) 0.11 mol/l bicarbonate-dithionite solution (BD-P), representing reductive-soluble P, mainly bound to Fe hydroxides; (3) 1 mol/l sodium hydroxide (NaOH), extracting metal-bound P, primarily associated with Fe and Al oxides (NaOH-SRP), and organic-bound P (NaOH-NRP); (4) 0.5 mol/l hydrochloric acid (HCl-P), targeting P bound in Ca carbonates and apatite; and (5) residual P.

Dissolved Fe concentrations in the NH 4 Cl, BD, and HCl extracts were determined by atomic absorption spectroscopy (Perkin Elmer 3330, Rodgau–Juegesheim, Germany). The residual Fe fraction was calculated as the difference between the total Fe content, measured by ICP-OES, and the sum of the NH 4 Cl, BD, and HCl fractions.

sections.heading: X-ray diffraction
paragraphs: X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses were performed on freeze-dried sediment samples that were manually ground using an agate mortar. Diffraction patterns were measured with a D2 Phaser diffractometer (Bruker), equipped with a Cobalt X-ray tube and an SSD160 detector, over a 2θ range of 10–90°, using a rotating sample holder (10 rpm). The step size was 0.014° 2θ, with a measurement time of 3.6 s per step. Mineral identification was conducted using DIFFRAC.EVA V5.2 software (Bruker) and the Crystallography Open Database (Gražulis et al.  12 ).

sections.heading: Scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM–EDX)
paragraphs: SEM–EDX (ICM 6000 Benchtop SEM, Jeol, Tokyo, Japan) was used to identify mineral phases in the sediment samples. After ultrasonic treatment, sediments were filtered using 0.4 µm polycarbonate filters. The filters were dried at 60 °C for 24 h and mounted on Al stubs. SEM–EDX analysis was performed at a working distance of 19 mm, with spot analyses conducted at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV using an energy-dispersive X-ray analyser (Jeol).

sections.heading: One-box model
paragraphs: A one-box model was applied to assess whether the development of sulphate concentrations in the lake is related to changes in atmospheric deposition. The application of the one-box model to lake sulphur budgets is described in Heinrich et al. ( 14 ). Details on its implementation for Lake Stechlin, including the parametrization, sulphur budget data and long-term atmospheric deposition data are provided in the Supplementary Information (Tables S1–S3).

sections.heading: Data processing and statistical analysis
paragraphs: Data analysis, statistical tests and graphical representations are based on Excel 2019 for Windows (Microsoft). Some graphics were edited using CorelDraw 2019 (Corel Corporation). Other software usages are explained in the respective chapters of the methods.

sections.heading: Sediment description and stratigraphic correlation
paragraphs: The analysed ~50 cm of sediment from the deepest point of Lake Stechlin (69.5 m) were dated using several time markers and comprise a sedimentation history of more than the last 100 years (Fig.  2 ). Contents of Pb, Zn, As, and Hg—used as proxies for industrial pollution beginning in the late 19th century—increased above a depth of 40 cm. Peak values corresponding to the  1960 s and  1970 s were observed at approximately 17 cm for Pb, 13 cm for Zn, 14–17 cm for As, and 16 cm for Hg. This chronology is supported by the maximum peak in  137 Cs activity at 15–16 cm, corresponding to the fallout-peak in 1963. The Ca peak at approximately 11–12 cm depth, attributed to autochthonous calcite (CaCO 3 ) precipitation, (see also Fig.  3 ) is used as a marker to broadly separate sediments deposited during the purely oligotrophic phase from those formed during the subsequent transition to increasingly mesotrophic conditions. The Ca peak coincides with a period of enhanced CaCO 3  and slightly increased P concentrations in the lake water during the late  1980 s to late  1990 s (IGB monitoring data,  https://fred.igb-berlin.de/ ). Fig. 2 Vertical distributions of TOC, Fe, P, Ca and S at the deepest site of Lake Stechlin (69.5 m). The right panel indicates sediment deposition age and trophic state (eu: eutrophic; oligo: oligotrophic) Fig. 3 A  Ti content [cps] and Ca content [wt.%] in seven sediment cores collected along a depth transect in Lake Stechlin. Stratigraphic correlation of sediments was based on the silty-sandy layer with high Ti (red area) content and increased pelagic calcite precipitation, as indicated by a rise in Ca (blue area).  B  Iron content and Fe/Ti ratios in seven sediment cores collected along a depth transect in Lake Stechlin.  C  Molar S to Fe ratios in seven sediment cores collected along a depth transect in Lake Stechlin

The highest Fe contents occur below 15 cm and decrease steadily toward the sediment surface. In the deeper, Fe-rich layers, the elevated mean P content is approximately 0.5 wt.% but shows substantial variability. In contrast, the P content is markedly lower between 10 and 21 cm (~0.14 wt.%) before increasing again in the upper, more recent sediments to values of ~0.5 wt.%. Sulphur shows a distinct peak (4.3 wt.%) at 16–17 cm and decreases to around 1 wt.% both above and below this depth. The upward decrease in S strongly correlates with the decline in Fe contents between 0 and 14 cm (R 2  = 0.987, n = 14). The sediments consist of dark, nearly black material with a dry mass content of 5%–12%. TOC contents are unusually high (> 25 wt.%) below 16 cm and decreases to ~10 wt.% in more recent sediments.

The Ti and Ca profiles allowed stratigraphic correlation of the sediment cores along the depth transect (Fig.  3 a). A distinct Ti–rich layer, indicative of sedimentological events associated with increased detrital input, was present in all cores, whereas elevated Ca contents marked the onset of enhanced pelagic calcite precipitation in the upper sediment section. The Ti peak was associated with a slightly brighter layer composed of silty-sandy material with a coarser grain size. It appeared at ~35 cm depth in cores from waters deeper than 56 m, and at around 25 cm and 18 cm in cores from shallower waters (51 m and 38 m, respectively). Increased calcite sedimentation began gradually between 16 and 8 cm. In cores from 69.5 to 65 m water depths, the top ~5 cm consisted of varves, which became thicker and more distinct with water depth. Sediments deposited since 2010 at the deepest site exhibit clearly visible diatom and Ca varves, described in more detail in Scholtysik et al. ( 47 ).

sections.heading: Sedimentary iron, phosphorus and sulphur
paragraphs: Between the Ti peak and the onset of calcite precipitation, i.e., during the oligotrophic phase discussed further, the sedimentary Fe contents increase with water depth, rising from approximately 1 wt.% at 38 m and 51 m to about 6–7 wt.% at 69.5 m (Fig.  3 b). Above the Ca-rich layer, i.e., during the increasingly mesotrophic phase, Fe content remained consistently low (approximately 1–2 wt.%) across all cores. A pronounced enrichment of Fe above typical sedimentological ratios, expressed by elevated Fe/Ti values, occurs between the Ti and Ca peaks, particularly in the cores from deeper waters, whereas this enrichment is less pronounced in the cores from shallower areas. Above the Ca peak, Fe/Ti ratios are uniformly low across all sites.

Sequential P and Fe fractionation revealed marked differences in the dominant binding forms between settling material, surface sediments with high S/Fe ratios, and deeper Fe-rich sediments with low to moderate S/Fe ratios from the deepest site (Figs.  3 c,  4 ). In the sediment traps deployed at 60 m, the dominant fraction was the reductive-soluble BD-TP, comprising approximately 75% of the total P, followed by HCl-TP (15%). With increasing sediment depth, there is initially a decrease in the BD-TP fraction. Samples from the relatively P-rich interval in the deeper sediment layers (24–30 cm) again exhibited an elevated proportion of BD-TP, accounting for ~50% of TP. The NaOH-SRP fraction is also enhanced in this interval, reaching approximately 18%. In contrast, the absolute amount of NaOH-NRP remained nearly constant across all samples (< 0.07 wt.%). The NH 4 Cl-P, HCl-P, and residual P (rest) fractions are consistently very low (< 0.03 wt.%). Fig. 4 Phosphorus and iron fractionation analysis of settling seston and sediments in 2018. The graph on the right shows the molar S/Fe ratios of the same material. The sediment material at 60 m was collected after two exposition periods. The sediment cores were taken in July 2018 (0–1 and 1–2 cm) and August 2018 (from 8 to 10 cm, core B) at the deepest site (69.5 m). NH 4 Cl-fraction: ‘pore water + adsorbed'; BD fraction: reductive-soluble ‘hydroxides’; NaOH-SRP fraction: metal-bound; NaOH-NRP fraction: organic-bound; HCl fraction: acid-soluble ‘carbonates’; and residual fraction (rest)

Total Fe contents in the settling material of the water column, determined from sediment trap samples in 60 m collected in two periods of late summer stratification 2018 (Fig.  4 , top), were 1.8 wt.% and 3.4 wt.%, respectively. In both samples, reductive-soluble BD-Fe represents the dominant fraction (~ 80%) with remainder mainly consisting of residual Fe (~ 20%). The HCl-Fe fraction is very small (< 2%) and the NH 4 Cl–Fe fraction is below the detection limit. In the P-rich interval at 24–30 cm sediment depth, the Fe content is considerably higher (about 7 wt.%, Fig.  4 ). Here, the HCl-soluble fraction was most abundant (55–60%), followed by residual Fe (30%) and the BD fraction (10%).

Because the stability of Fe–P phases depends on sulphide activity in sediments (Rothe et al.  43 ), the S/Fe ratio was used as a proxy for Fe sulphide dominance (Fig.  3 c). In cores from water depths greater than 56 m, the S/Fe ratio is generally below 0.5 in sediments deeper than 20 cm, but the ratio increases towards the sediment–water interface to values exceeding 2.0. Detailed analysis of solid Fe forms confirms the presence of framboidal pyrite at 17–18 cm sediment depth in the 69.5 m core, where the S/Fe ratio is elevated (1.2) (Fig.  S2 ).

sections.heading: X-ray diffraction and microscopic observations
paragraphs: Mineralogical analyses of the deep (< 20 cm) Fe- and P-rich sediment layers from the deepest lake site indicated the presence of calcite, quartz, vivianite, siderite, and pyrite. Additionally, a Ca–Fe–Mg–Mn-rich carbonate mineral, interpreted as an ankerite-like phase, was identified. Its chemical formula, calculated using the Rietveld method, was CaFe 0.68 Mg 0.27 Mn 0.05 [CO 3 ] 2 . At 8.5–9.5 cm core depth, where P content was low, only quartz, calcite, and pyrite were detected, and no other crystalline Fe minerals were identified. Compared to the 23.5–24.5 cm interval, calcite peaks at 8.5–9.5 cm were more intense, whereas peaks corresponding to the ankerite-like carbonate and vivianite were absent. Microscope observations revealed vivianite in all sediment cores collected from water depths > 56 m. Vivianite was particularly abundant in the interval between the Ca and Ti peaks, where the S/Fe ratio (Fig.  3 ) was below ~ 0.5. Blue vivianite crystal aggregates (Fig.  S1 ) were frequently observed in association with rusty-coloured particles (Fig.  5 ). Fig. 5 X-ray diffractograms of sediments from depths 8.5–9.5 cm and 23.5–24.5 cm at the deepest site (69.5 m, core A). V: vivianite, A: ankerite, C: calcite, Q: quartz, P: pyrite, and S: siderite. The 2θ peak positions and their relative intensities are reported in Table S4 in the Supplementary Information

sections.heading: Particle sedimentation recorded by sediment traps
paragraphs: The recent dynamics of Fe sedimentation has changed markedly with the beginning of eutrophication and the associated redox shift in the hypolimnion. Beginning in 2016, pronounced seasonal peaks in Fe sedimentation rates (up to 35 mg Fe m −2  d −1 ) were recorded in the 60 m trap between November and January (Fig.  6 ). These peaks coincided with the end of the stagnation period, when dissolved O 2  concentrations below 60 m declined to nearly 0 mg l −1 . The annual Fe flux at 20 m declined from 4.38 ± 0.54 (2010–2012) to 1.84 ± 0.44 mg Fe m −2  d −1  (2016–2018) due to reduced Fe contents in settling particles. In contrast, mean Fe sedimentation rates at 60 m remained stable over time (2010–2012: 10.54 ± 5.02, 2016–2018: 11.67 ± 2.58 mg Fe m −2  d −1 ). The maximum Fe content recorded in the 60 m trap was 3.2 wt.% (Fig. S3), while mean annual values were 0.90 ± 0.37 wt.% for 2010–2012) and 0.96 ± 0.12 wt.% for 2016–2018). These values are consistent with the Fe content observed at the sediment surface (see Figs.  2 ,  4 , and  6 ). Fig. 6 Vertical Fe fluxes at 20 m and 60 m water depths, measured using sediment traps deployed at the deepest site of Lake Stechlin (69.5 m) in 2010–2012 and 2016–2018, respectively. Mean annual Fe contents for the two periods are indicated in the legend. Hatched bars indicate periods for which annual fluxes were calculated from incomplete trap deployments/interpolated sampling intervals

sections.heading: Porewater concentrations of dissolved iron and sulphate
paragraphs: Analysis of the porewater iron and sulphate concentrations indicate that sulphidic conditions prevailed in the bottom sediments during the recent past. In the deepest part of the lake, the dissolved Fe concentrations in the water directly overlying the sediment were close to zero (Fig.  7 , left). Within the upper 10 cm of the sediment, dissolved Fe consistently remained below 1 mg l −1 , but increased to higher values between 2 and 8 mg l −1  at a depth of 30 cm. Similarly, low Fe concentrations within the top 10 cm were found at a depth of 30 m (0.22 ± 0.23 mg l −1 , n = 40) and at a depth of 17 m (0.58 ± 0.23 mg l −1 , n = 10) (data available under:  https://fred.igb-berlin.de/ ). Sulphate concentration profiles exhibited a sharp gradient at the sediment–water interface, with decreasing concentrations toward the sediment (Fig.  7 , right). In the deeper anoxic porewater, sulphate concentrations ranged from 1.2 to 8 mg l −1 . In the overlying water, sulphate concentrations showed a slight declining trend between 2009 and 2017/18, consistent with routine monitoring data from the water column (see Fig.  8 ). Fig. 7 Concentrations of dissolved Fe and sulphate in the porewater (grey area) and in the water above the sediment at the deepest point (69.5 m), measured using dialysis samplers from 2009 to 2018 Fig. 8 Atmospheric sulphate deposition rates at the lake and across the entire catchment, compared with modelled sulphate input into the lake, calculated using a one-box model for the period 1970–2020. Sulphate input was modelled by fitting the simulated sulphate concentration curve (blue line) to the measured values (circles)

The sulphate reduction and diffusion rates (Table  1 ) were derived from porewater profiles shown in Fig.  7  and from additional measurements. No systematic seasonal or long-term variations in these rates could be identified with the available dataset. However, sulphate reduction rates were significantly higher in the deeper areas of the lake (69.5 and 58 m) than at shallower sites (17 and 30 m), despite comparable sulphate availability across these depths (see Table  1 ). The area-weighted estimate of the lake-wide mean sulphate reduction rate yielded a value of approximately 70 mg SO 4 2−  m −2  d −1 .

sections.heading: Modelling of sulphur input by one-box model
paragraphs: Because the formation of pyrite (FeS₂) depends on the availability of sulphur and can substantially deplete sulphate pools, long-term changes in sulphate concentrations were examined. In 2020, the sulphate concentration in Lake Stechlin was approximately 32 mg l −1 , representing a gradual decline from 40 mg l −1  since 2000, when continuous monitoring began (Fig.  8 ). Two isolated measurements from 1970 and 1985, which recorded concentrations of 11 and 20 mg l −1 , respectively, indicate that sulphate levels more than doubled by the end of the 20th century. A marked increase in sulphate concentration occurred after 1985, with maximum values observed in the measurement series from 2000 onwards. Atmospheric SO 2  concentration measured at a monitoring station near Lake Stechlin remained relatively high between 1974 and approximately 1987 (around 20 µg/m 3 ), before declining sharply to below 5 µg/m 3  during the  1990 s (Table S3). Figure  8  presents estimates of atmospheric S deposition rates on the lake surface and across the entire catchment area. Simulations using the one-box model indicate that actual sulphur inputs to the lake catchment area exceeded direct atmospheric deposition onto the lake surface. During the period of high sulphur loading, modelled S input was lower than the atmospheric deposition in the entire catchment area. However, after 1987, the modelled inputs exceeded atmospheric deposition to the entire catchment and declined more slowly than the measured deposition rates. The measured sulphur deposition in the catchment between 1970 and 2000 was 5.56 × 10 3  kg ha −1 , closely aligning with the modelled input of 5.91 × 10 3  kg ha −1 . Despite uncertainties related to S retention rate derived from a single dated sediment core from the deepest point and from incomplete monitoring data, the modelling results support robust conclusions regarding long-term sulphur dynamics in the lake.

sections.heading: Geochemical focusing and enrichment of Fe at the deepest site
paragraphs: The sediment stratigraphy is characterised by two prominent markers: (i) a coarser-grained layer in the lower section characterized by a distinctive Ti peak and (ii) the onset of significant calcite precipitation in the upper 15 cm interval, indicated by a distinct Ca peak (Fig.  3 ). All geochemical changes discussed here occurred between these stratigraphic boundaries, which are supported by heavy metal and radiochemical dating.

Elevated Fe/Ti ratios demonstrate pronounced Fe enrichment in sediments deposited at water depths > 56 m (Fig.  3 ). This Fe enrichment strongly declined no later than the  1960 s, approximately coinciding with the onset of significant calcite deposition at ~15 cm (core A1, Fig.  2 ). A similar pattern in Lake Stechlin sediments has been reported by Röper and Schwarz ( 42 ): Sediments deposited since the Boreal (i.e., since 9800 BP) at a water depth of 68 m showed significantly higher Fe contents (up to 10 wt.%, average ~5 wt.%) than those at a water depth of 36 m (average ~1.5 wt.%). These findings suggest that sediments older than those analysed in the present study were also enriched in Fe at greater water depths. As enhanced erosion or other external inputs can be excluded for the past century, the observed Fe enrichment must have resulted from internal redistribution processes, as indicated by the Fe/Ti ratio. We attribute this Fe enrichment to “geochemical focusing” according to Schaller and Wehrli ( 45 ). This enrichment involves a sequence of geochemical processes: (i) reductive dissolution of solid phases such as FeO x  in shallow sediments, (ii) diffusion of dissolved Fe into the water column, (iii) dispersion and oxidation within the oxic water column, and (iv) eventual transport with subsequent deposition at the deepest site (Fig.  9 ). Fig. 9 Schematic representation of geochemical processes involved in the focusing of Fe in Lake Stechlin. These processes led to the formation of vivianite (top), contrasted with the post-1960 situation (bottom), where pyrite formed instead of vivianite. In the lower left side, a simplified profile of P vs. S/Fe is presented: the upper P content in a sediment profile is considered “temporary”, because it does not get buried below a certain depth as a stable mineral phase that could withstand a deeper burial

In our conceptual model, geochemical focussing was initiated by reductive dissolution of FeO x  at the sediment–water interface across all water depths and was likely facilitated by the high organic carbon content (Fig.  9 ), which favoured reducing conditions. The occurrence of organic-rich sediments in a formerly oligotrophic lake can be attributed to allochthonous inputs from the surrounding forest combined with minimal dilution by minerogenic material. Under these conditions, FeO x  minerals were likely reduced shortly after sedimentation, and the resulting dissolved Fe diffused back into the water column, where it was dispersed. A strong contrast between anoxic, organic-rich surface sediments and an oxic water column appears to have been a prerequisite for the export of dissolved Fe from sediments and its subsequent oxidation in the oxic water column (Scholz et al.  49 ). Such redox gradients are common in stratified lakes irrespective of trophic state (e.g. Steinsberger et al.  52 ). In eutrophic lakes, during stratification, the oxycline shifts upward from the sediment into the overlying water column, where Fe can be reprecipitated. Short-term redox oscillations driven by internal seiches likely further enhanced repeated dissolution- precipitation processes (Valerio et al.  53 ).

Water movement or turbulent (eddy-like) diffusion likely facilitated lateral redistribution of Fe particles towards deeper areas, where Fe particles tend to sink due to gravity rather than being transported to shallower zones (Schaller and Wehrli  45 ; Raiswell and Anderson  41 ). This restriction of final burial to a small profundal area (> 56 m, comprising 3.95% of the total lake area) and comparatively low sedimentation rates enhanced this focusing effect by limiting dilution. Together, these sedimentary and hydrodynamic controls established a persistent focusing regime that governed long-term Fe and P burial.

The long-term burial of Fe and total P at the deepest site was facilitated by diagenetic transformation of Fe into more stable and dissolution-resistant phases (Figs.  4  and  5 ). This process was partly associated with the formation of vivianite, which was identified in sediments below 56 m water depth (Figs.  5  and  S1 ). Under non-sulphidic anoxic conditions, the enrichment of Fe hydroxides and adsorbed P served as a precursor to P sequestration via vivianite formation (Heinrich et al.  13 ). Additionally, a substantial HCl-soluble fraction and the occurrence of an ankerite-like mineral suggest incorporation of Fe in Fe-rich carbonates (Figs.  4  and  5 ).

sections.heading: Decline of long-term geochemical Fe focusing
paragraphs: The decrease in Fe contents within the upper ~20 cm of the deep-water sediments reflects reduced Fe release from shallower areas. This marks a strong decline of geochemical focusing and coincides with increasing fixation of Fe as FeSₓ (e.g., pyrite), as reflected by rising S/Fe ratios across all water depths (Fig.  3 c). Consequently, less Fe became available for redistribution and accumulation at the deeper areas.

During the period of Fe focusing, sediments retained sufficient Fe to support the formation of both FeS x  and other Fe minerals such as vivianite. As sulphate reduction intensified and Fe availability declined, FeS x  formation became dominant, progressively suppressing vivianite formation. The increase in the S/Fe ratios from ~0.2 before ~1950 to ~2.0 since the ~1960s indicates the establishment of increasingly sulphidic conditions (Fig.  3 ). Decreasing total S contents in the uppermost sediments (Fig.  2 ) further suggest that the sediment’s capacity for S fixation as FeS x  was largely exhausted. Fluctuations in Fe and total P contents below 20 cm depth indicate a variable intensity of vivianite formation during this period (Fig.  2 ).

Importantly, the decline of geochemical focusing, concomitant with declining of Fe contents in younger sediments (~0–20 cm), cannot be synchronised with recent trophic changes. Fe contents began to decline already in the  1960 s, when the lake was still oligotrophic and deep-water conditions remained oxic (Fig.  2 ). At present, temporary bottom-water sulphidation during late summer stagnation and highly sulphidic porewaters (Scholtysik et al.  47 ) prevent upward Fe diffusion, consistent with the absence of dissolved Fe in surface sediments (Fig.  7 ). Sulphidic conditions have been documented not only at the deepest site but also at water depths of 32 m and 0.5 m (Sass et al.  44 ). This interpretation is also supported by the relatively high S/Fe ratios in the surface sediments (0–2 cm) at depths between 5 and 30 m (Table S5), which are typical of more sulphidic conditions.

Sediment-trap data indicate that Fe redistribution is still observed in the modern lake, but that its character has changed. The sediment-trap-based budget indicated a shift in the relative contributions of Fe redistribution between the two observation periods. During 2010–2012, most of the excess Fe flux at 60 m could be explained by mechanically focused Fe-bearing particles. In contrast, during 2016–2018, 70.3% of the excess Fe flux was operationally attributed to a geochemical redistribution component. The larger difference in Fe fluxes between the 20 m and 60 m traps during 2016–2018 was mainly caused by the decline in Fe sedimentation at 20 m, which resulted from lower Fe contents in the settling material (Fig.  6 ). Whether this decline results from altered hydrology (Pöschke et al.  39 ) or enhanced Fe retention in littoral sediments due to sulphidation cannot be resolved with the available data.

sections.heading: Drivers of increased sulphate reduction
paragraphs: The decline of Fe focusing since the  1960 s implies intensified sulphate reduction, which promoted sulphide formation and shifting Fe burial toward FeS x  formation. Potential controlling factors include reducing conditions, the availability of degradable OM, and sulphate supply (Berner  4 ; Westrich and Berner  54 ; Holmer and Storkholm  18 ).

Because the sediments of Lake Stechlin are unusually rich in OM across all sediments depths (Fig.  2 ), and the absence of a correlation between OM and sulphate reduction rates (Table  1 ), limitation by OM quantity appears unlikely. However, decreasing contents of reactive Fe oxides may have stimulated sulphate reduction by reducing OM preservation via Fe association (Lalonde et al.  28 ; Barber et al.  2 ), and by reduced competition between microbial Fe reduction and sulphate reduction for easily degradable OM (Lovley and Phillips  33 ). Changes in the OM quality, resulting from altered terrestrial inputs or shifts in macrophyte communities (Hilt et al.  15 ), may further modulate reduction pathways.

Increased sulphate availability provides an additional explanation. FeSₓ formation, and P mobilization in lake sediments is increased sulphate availability, as suggested by numerous studies (see review by Zak et al.  59 ). Sulphate concentrations in Lake Stechlin have risen (Fig.  8 ), consistent with regional trends linked to atmospheric deposition associated with fossil fuel combustion and industrialization, as well as to sulphate inputs from the drainage of mines or wetlands (Brimblecombe  5 ; Zak et al.  59 ).

Despite the increase, sulphate concentrations of Lake Stechlin (~30 mg l −1 ) remained relatively low compared to other natural lakes in the region, which ranged from 0.5 to 424 mg l −1  between 2015 and 2018 (median: 52.2 mg l −1 , n = 421; data from Zak et al.  59 ). One-box modelling indicates that direct atmospheric deposition alone cannot explain the observed increase (Fig.  8 ). Delayed sulphate transport from the catchment is therefore likely. Overall, the amount of sulphur deposited atmospherically across the entire catchment corresponded reasonably well with the modelled sulphate inputs since 1970. Although atmospheric pollution began already in the early twentieth century, the delayed and moderate increase in sulphate concentrations in Lake Stechlin after 1970 may be partly reflected by efficient buffering by Fe compounds prior to 1960’s (Chapter 4.1).

sections.heading: Implication for internal P cycling
paragraphs: The decline of Fe focusing influenced P diagenesis and retention in three main ways: (1) Declining Fe availability limited vivianite formation, as reflected by elevated S/Fe ratios (Fig.  3 ) and low dissolved Fe concentrations in porewaters (Fig.  7 ). Because vivianite formation was spatially restricted and Fe declined gradually (Fig.  3 ), this shift did not immediately increase water-column P. (2) Fe sulphide formation inhibited the upward transport of Fe 2+  to the sediment surface and its subsequent oxidation to Fe hydroxides. While this process may influence short- term P dynamics, it is less important for long-term P sequestration under permanent anoxic conditions (Gächter and Müller  10 ). (3) Vivianite-P may dissolve under sulphidic conditions, a process that is currently under investigation (Kubeneck et al.  26 ; Van Kuppevelt et al.  27 ). In Lake Stechlin, however, the quantitative contribution of vivianite dissolution to water column P is likely minor due to the limited spatial extent of vivianite-rich sediments and the separation between sulphate reduction zones and deeper vivianite layers.

Although the results demonstrate weakened sedimentary P-Fe coupling, their quantitative impact on the internal P budget of Lake Stechlin remains uncertain due to spatial heterogeneity among lake compartments and temporal variability in littoral sink-source dynamics (Holdt et al.  17 ). Recent studies indicate that increasing lake-water P concentration is primarily driven by changes in the macrophyte communities, leading to the shift of the littoral zone from a P sink to a P source (Gonsiorczyk et al.  11 , Hilt et al. 2025). Nevertheless, the weakening of sedimentary P-Fe binding due to Fe sulphidation has rendered the lake ecosystem more vulnerable to additional P inputs from the littoral or external sources. Furthermore, progressive Fe sulphidation in littoral sediments may further reduce their capacity to retain P, thereby amplifying the role of the shallow zone as a P source and as a driver of changes in the lake`s trophic status.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Under non-sulphidic, oligotrophic conditions, reactive Fe underwent geochemical focusing, resulting in Fe enrichment in sediments at the lake’s deepest site. Fe burial was facilitated by the formation of authigenic minerals within the sediment, such as ankerite and the Fe-phosphate mineral vivianite. Excessive P accumulation at the sediment surface under oligotrophic conditions and oxic water columns promoted the formation of stable P compounds like vivianite once the sediments became buried and anoxic.

Since porewater became sulphidic, presumably around  1960 s, Fe has been predominantly immobilised as pyrite, thereby preventing its redeposition from shallower sediments to deeper zones. This shift inhibited the formation of vivianite and other Fe phosphate minerals and strongly reduced geochemical Fe focusing. The underlying causes of enhanced sulphide formation driven by sulphate reduction could not be resolved unequivocally. Sulphate reduction may have been stimulated either by increased availability of degradable OM or by elevated sulphate concentrations, as documented in Lake Stechlin and numerous lakes globally.

Over the last century, increased atmospheric deposition across the catchment has continuously supplied sulphate to the lake, even after a pronounced decline in air pollution. However, the onset of extensive pyrite formation cannot be directly linked to the strong eutrophication observed since 2012. Over several decades, the gradual decline in Fe controlled P-binding capacity did not measurably affect the lake’s P balance, as external P input from the largely forested catchment remained low. Once P release from the littoral zone increased, this additional P load could no longer be compensated for, owing to the weakened Fe-controlled burial of P in the sediments.
